extracted.intended_audience: federal judges, magistrate judges, and patent litigators managing patent cases
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for managing early patent-litigation procedures, with emphasis on claim construction, discovery timing, contention disclosures, standing/ownership issues, and case-management practices to promote efficiency and prevent abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim construction is based on the patent claims, specification, prosecution history, and, in some cases, on extrinsic evidence to reconstruct what patent claim terms would have meant to a person skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intrinsic evidence (claims, specification, prosecution history) is primary; extrinsic evidence (including inventor testimony) is typically given less weight but can illuminate context, background, and prosecution events. Courts should consider which sources are necessary to meaningfully construe terms and avoid abstract constructions that do not affect outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight and use of inventor testimony and expert evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor’s testimony is typically seen as extrinsic evidence and given less weight, particularly when self-serving; Teva expanded the use of expert declarations and testimony in claim construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because Teva allows greater use of expert evidence on subsidiary factual determinations, courts should ask early whether parties intend to rely on expert testimony and its substance. Courts may allow expert tutorials and reserve the option to take expert evidence if factual disputes arise; consider methods like the 'hot tub' to have opposing experts address each other to clarify disputed issues and credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitting fact discovery prior to claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Permitting fact discovery in advance of claim construction helps focus claims and defenses because knowledge of accused product structure and relevant prior art often determines which claim terms need construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-claim-construction discovery is common and often mandated by local patent rules (e.g., early disclosures of infringement and invalidity contentions). Courts should discuss potential limits or phasing to avoid wasteful discovery on issues unrelated to claim construction (e.g., damages, equitable defenses, willfulness) when a claim-construction ruling could be dispositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact discovery after claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: As a result of a court’s claim-construction order, issues often arise which justify additional fact discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most courts set fact discovery to proceed for a period after the ruling. Inventor depositions for Markman purposes are sometimes initially limited to claim-construction topics, with broader depositions allowed after the Markman process completes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of expert discovery relative to claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert reports on infringement, invalidity, and damages are central; technical experts opine based on the meaning of claim terms as determined by (or anticipated from) the court’s claim-construction order. For this reason, claim construction should precede expert reports and depositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many courts schedule expert discovery and depositions to begin after claim construction. Other courts set expert discovery before claim construction but require experts to write reports in the alternative relative to each side’s proposed constructions. Courts should structure expert scheduling to reflect whether claim scope will materially affect expert analyses (including damages).

rubrics_metrics.name: Modifying legal contentions after claim construction (good-cause requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many courts allow parties to modify their infringement and invalidity contentions after claim construction, but require a 'timely showing of good cause' to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local patent rules and case law (e.g., O2 Micro) require diligence to establish 'good cause'; failure to investigate prior art early enough risks exclusion of that evidence. Courts should balance preventing sandbagging with avoiding unfair traps where court constructions differ from party proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction before summary judgment (or combined with it)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim construction is a critical predicate to the most common summary judgment motions; most courts complete claim construction first, before allowing dispositive motions, on the theory parties need a definitive statement of claim scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some courts combine claim construction with summary judgment (especially motions that turn primarily on claim construction) to increase efficiency; others require explanation of the significance of competing constructions and limit later alternative theories. Courts should account for burden of drafting summary-judgment motions under multiple potential constructions and consider appellate ripeness concerns (Federal Circuit views on developing factual record).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of early, limited claim construction to encourage settlement
rubrics_metrics.description: Early, separate claim construction (sometimes limited to a subset of case-dispositive terms) can facilitate settlement by recalibrating parties’ assessments of exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may schedule settlement conferences shortly after a claim-construction order. Use this procedure only where a party persuasively shows the case largely turns on a discrete issue; otherwise there is potential for strategic abuse by defendants or tactical resistance by plaintiffs seeking nuisance-value leverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary claim construction for preliminary injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Preliminary injunction motions in patent cases typically require a court to construe claim terms on an accelerated schedule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preliminary constructions are less informed (less discovery) and are not binding; courts may later reconsider and revise constructions applied during preliminary-injunction decisions as more detailed briefing/record is developed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early document production requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Local patent rules in several districts require parties to produce infringement and/or invalidity-related documents with their initial disclosures or very early in a case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include N.D. Ill. LPRs 2.1–2.4, W.D. Tenn. LPR 3.1, and N.D. Ohio LPRs 3.1–3.2. Plaintiffs often favor early production but must be careful not to let early obligations disadvantage them (e.g., exposing invalidity materials).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership and standing document production
rubrics_metrics.description: Several jurisdictions require plaintiffs to produce all documents relating to ownership of the asserted patents (or more broadly, documents relating to the standing of the party alleging infringement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This contemplates production of assignment and licensing documents where exclusive licensees may be bringing suit. Courts and local rules (e.g., N.D. Cal. Patent L.R. 3-2(d)) often enforce thorough production to resolve standing questions early.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff must hold all substantial patent rights to sue
rubrics_metrics.description: A party suing for infringement must hold exclusive rights to the patent being asserted; only a patentee (or an assignee) may bring an action for patent infringement. Exclusive licensees may sue only if they hold 'all substantial rights.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts look to the intention of the parties and the substance of what was retained by the owner versus granted. Oral agreements cannot transfer 'all substantial rights.' Exclusive licensees lacking all substantial rights may need the patentee as a co-plaintiff.

rubrics_metrics.name: All joint patent owners must be joined as plaintiffs
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinarily, all co-owners of a patent must consent/join as plaintiffs for an infringement suit to be maintained; ownership depends on 'the substance of what was granted' through assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a co-owner is not joined and ownership is disputed, courts may dismiss the complaint (typically without prejudice) until the defect is corrected. Exceptions to involuntary joinder are narrow (e.g., exclusive licensee seeking to join patent owner, or waiver by agreement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive licensee obligations (joining licensor)
rubrics_metrics.description: An exclusive licensee who has less than all substantial rights may have standing to sue but frequently must join the patent owner as a necessary party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may grant leave to amend to add patent owner as co-plaintiff rather than dismiss outright. The presence or absence of rights (territorial limitations, retained licensing rights) determines procedural posture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonexclusive licensee has no standing
rubrics_metrics.description: A nonexclusive or 'bare' license confers no constitutional standing under the Patent Act to bring suit or to join a suit with the patentee because such a licensee suffers no legal injury from infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties and courts should examine the license scope; where only a covenant not to sue exists, the licensee cannot invoke patent-act standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment and conveyance of right to sue require transfer of substantially all rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignment of a patent, or an exclusive license that conveys substantially all patent rights, conveys the right to sue for present and future infringement. Transfer of the right to sue for past infringement requires contractual manifestation of that intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts analyze assignment language under applicable state contract law and do not require any particular formula of words. Determination focuses on substance, not form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covenant not to sue can moot a controversy
rubrics_metrics.description: Issuing a covenant not to sue or making a similarly binding representation such that the asserting party could not reasonably be expected to resume enforcement renders the declaratory-judgment action moot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have applied this principle (e.g., Already v. Nike) and may dismiss actions when judicially binding assurances make a controversy nonjusticiable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dismissal for lack of standing generally without prejudice
rubrics_metrics.description: If a case must be dismissed for lack of standing, it should ordinarily be dismissed without prejudice so the plaintiff can correct the defect (e.g., join co-owners).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the basis for dismissal cannot be rectified (e.g., covenant not to sue moots the controversy), dismissal should be with prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of joint-infringement roles in contentions
rubrics_metrics.description: Where joint direct infringement is alleged, a patentee must describe 'the role of each such party in the direct infringement' in infringement contentions under many local patent rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Districts with such requirements include N.D. Cal., D. Idaho, N.D. Ill., Maryland, E.D. Mo., D. Nev., and others. Clear mapping of accused actors to claim elements is expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phased winnowing of asserted prior art references
rubrics_metrics.description: To rein in excessive asserted prior art, a phased process is proposed: a Preliminary Election of Asserted Prior Art (no more than 12 references per patent and total 40) followed by a Final Election (no more than 6 references per patent and total 20).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model Order Limiting Excess Patent Claims and Prior Art (Fed. Cir. Advisory Council) recommends these numeric limits (with some relaxation when only one patent is asserted). Other courts (e.g., D. Utah) counsel reducing final disclosures to a manageable subset, often no more than three references per claim as a general rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optional local-rule practices (summary judgment, oral-advice summaries, damages, licenses, bifurcation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Less common PLR provisions include requiring summary judgment motions as part of claim-construction, producing written summaries of oral advice when waiver of privilege is alleged, requiring damages disclosures after Markman, producing license agreements, and district variation in bifurcation practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: D. Utah LPR 6.2 (SJ as part of claim construction); S.D. Cal. P.L.R. 3.7(b) (produce summary of oral advice if waiver); S.D. Ind. CMP (damages statement within 30 days after Markman); S.D. Tex. P.R. 3-2(a)(4) (produce license agreements); S.D. Ohio always bifurcates willfulness, N.D. Ga. disfavors liability/damages bifurcation, W.D.N.C. suggests considering bifurcation. Courts should consider these tools to manage case scope and costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early case-management exploration of business relationships and technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Given that patent complaints are often sparse, courts may find it helpful to explore parties’ prior dealings, business relationships (e.g., licensing history), and market/technology considerations in an early case-management or settlement conference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding these contextual factors and the nature/complexity of the technology can inform whether adopting variations on patent local rules or other tailored case-management strategies will aid efficient resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleading standards post-2015 (Twombly/Iqbal govern patent complaints)
rubrics_metrics.description: With the abolition of Rule 84 and Form 18, the pleading standards set forth in Twombly and Iqbal now govern patent cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent complaints must satisfy the plausibility standard from Twombly/Iqbal rather than relying on the prior Form 18; this can affect early motion practice (motions to dismiss) and the level of factual detail courts may explore at initial conferences.
